title: The Flower
tagline: A bisexual flower, its four whorls, types of inflorescence and placentation — the structure behind reproduction in flowering plants.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The flower is the reproductive shoot of a flowering plant, and its structure is one of the most regular and most frequently examined topics in ICSE Class IX Biology. This chapter begins with a typical bisexual flower and its four whorls — calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium — then moves to the parts of a flower in outline, the arrangement of flowers into inflorescences, and the way the ovary is attached to the ovary wall, known as placentation. The emphasis is on being able to name each part, say where it is, and relate it to its role in reproduction.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: A bisexual flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium

facts.label: Androecium
facts.value: Male whorl made of stamens; each stamen has a filament and an anther

facts.label: Gynoecium
facts.value: Female whorl made of one or more carpels; each carpel has stigma, style and ovary

learn.title: A bisexual flower and its four whorls

blocks.text: A typical bisexual flower is built on a swollen tip of the stalk called the thalamus, or receptacle, on which the floral parts are arranged in concentric circles called whorls. From outside to inside, the four whorls are the calyx, the corolla, the androecium and the gynoecium. The calyx is the outermost whorl, made of sepals, which are usually green and protect the flower in the bud stage. The corolla is the next whorl, made of petals, which are often coloured and help attract insects. The androecium is the male whorl, made of stamens, each of which has a filament and an anther that produces pollen. The gynoecium is the female whorl, made of one or more carpels; each carpel has a stigma, a style and an ovary. A flower that has both androecium and gynoecium is bisexual; one that has only one of them is unisexual.

items.meaning: A flower that contains both androecium and gynoecium, so it has both male and female parts.
A flower that has only androecium or only gynoecium.
The swollen tip of the flower stalk on which the floral whorls are arranged.
The outermost whorl of a flower, made of sepals.
The whorl of petals inside the calyx.
The male whorl of a flower, made of stamens.
The female whorl of a flower, made of one or more carpels.
The female reproductive unit of a flower, consisting of stigma, style and ovary.

items: The four whorls of a bisexual flower are calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx = sepals; corolla = petals; androecium = stamens; gynoecium = carpels.
A stamen has a filament and an anther; the anther produces pollen.
A carpel has a stigma, a style and an ovary; the ovary contains ovules.
A bisexual flower has both male and female whorls; a unisexual flower has only one.
The thalamus is the platform on which the floral parts are seated.

items.text: A Hibiscus flower is a familiar bisexual example with a prominent stalked stigma, long staminal column and five petals.
items.note: The parts are visible and separable, which is why it is a good classroom specimen.

items.text: Maize has unisexual flowers: the tassel bears male flowers and the ear bears female flowers.
items.note: Unisexual flowers are common in some important crops.

learn.title: Parts of a flower and their details

blocks.text: Beyond the four whorls, it is useful to know the smaller parts in outline. A sepal may be free from the others or fused with them; when the sepals are free the calyx is called polysepalous, and when they are fused it is gamosepalous. The same idea applies to petals: free petals give a polypetalous corolla, and fused petals give a gamopetalous corolla. The anther is usually bilobed and each lobe has two pollen sacs, so a typical anther has four pollen sacs in which pollen grains develop. The ovary may have one or many chambers, called locules, and inside each locule are one or more ovules attached to a part of the ovary wall called the placenta. When the flower is pollinated, the pollen lands on the stigma, grows a pollen tube down the style and reaches the ovary, where fertilisation takes place and the ovules become seeds.

items.meaning: A unit of the calyx, usually green and protective in the bud.
A unit of the corolla, often coloured and attractive to pollinators.
Male part of the flower, made of a filament and an anther.
The male gametophyte of a flowering plant, produced in the anther.
Female part of the flower: stigma, style and ovary with ovules.
Structure inside the ovary that becomes a seed after fertilisation.
A chamber of the ovary.

items: A typical anther has four pollen sacs, two in each lobe.
Pollen grains are produced in the pollen sacs of the anther.
The ovary may be unilocular or multilocular, with one or many ovules.
The placenta is the part of the ovary wall to which the ovules are attached.
After pollination, the pollen tube grows through the style to reach the ovary.
Free parts are described as polysepalous or polypetalous; fused parts as gamosepalous or gamopetalous.

items.text: In a pea flower the petals are often partly fused into a keel, showing gamopetalous arrangement.
items.note: The same family can show both free and fused forms in different flowers.

items.text: A pomegranate ovary is multilocular with many ovules, which become the many seeds in the fruit.
items.note: Number of locules and ovules is a useful detail in describing a flower.

blocks.text: A flower does not always stand alone on a stalk; often several flowers are arranged together on a common axis. This arrangement is called an inflorescence. The main axis may keep growing and produce flowers laterally, or it may end in a flower and stop growing. The two broad patterns are the racemose and the cymose types. In racemose inflorescences the main axis continues to grow and the flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal order, meaning the older flowers are below and the younger ones above. In cymose inflorescences the main axis ends in a flower, so growth is limited, and the flowers are borne in a basipetal order, meaning the older flowers are above and the younger ones below. Examples of racemose inflorescence include the raceme, corymb and umbel; examples of cymose inflorescence include the monochasial and dichasial cyme.

items.meaning: The arrangement of flowers on a common floral axis.
Inflorescence in which the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal order.
Inflorescence in which the main axis ends in a flower and flowers are borne in basipetal order.
Arrangement in which younger flowers are towards the apex and older ones towards the base.
Arrangement in which younger flowers are towards the base and older ones towards the apex.

items: An inflorescence is an arrangement of several flowers on a common axis.
In racemose types the main axis continues to grow and flowers are lateral.
In cymose types the main axis ends in a flower and growth is limited.
Racemose flowers open in acropetal order; cymose flowers open in basipetal order.
Common racemose forms include raceme, corymb and umbel.
Common cymose forms include monochasial and dichasial cymes.

items.text: Mustard and radish show a raceme-type racemose inflorescence with flowers on short stalks along a long axis.
items.note: A raceme is one of the commonest inflorescence types students recognise.

items.text: Some flowers appear in flat-topped clusters that are easier to describe after learning the rules of arrangement.
items.note: The cluster shape follows from whether the axis keeps growing or ends in a flower.

blocks.text: The ovary is the most important part of the gynoecium because it contains the ovules from which seeds develop. Inside the ovary, the ovules are attached to the ovary wall at a region called the placenta. The arrangement of the placentae and ovules within the ovary is called placentation, and it is a useful characteristic in describing and identifying flowers. In marginal placentation the ovary is one-chambered and the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture, with ovules borne on it, as in the pea. In axile placentation the ovary has two or more chambers and the placentae are in the centre where the septa meet, as in the china rose and tomato. In parietal placentation the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on peripheral placentae, as in mustard and cucumber. In basal placentation the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and bears a single ovule, as in sunflower and marigold. In free-central placentation the ovules are borne on a central column not connected to the ovary wall by septa, as in carnation and Dianthus.

items.meaning: The region of the ovary wall to which the ovules are attached.
The arrangement of placentae and ovules inside the ovary.
Ovules borne on a ridge along the ventral suture of a one-chambered ovary; example: pea.
Ovules borne on placentae in the centre of a multilocular ovary; example: china rose, tomato.
Ovules borne on the inner wall or on peripheral placentae; example: mustard, cucumber.
A single ovule attached at the base of the ovary; example: sunflower, marigold.
Ovules borne on a central column free from the ovary wall; example: Dianthus, carnation.

items: Placentation means the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary.
In marginal placentation the ovary is unilocular and the placenta is a ventral ridge; example: pea.
In axile placentation the ovary is multilocular with central placentae; example: china rose, tomato.
In parietal placentation the ovules lie on the inner wall; example: mustard, cucumber.
In basal placentation a single ovule is at the base; example: sunflower, marigold.
In free-central placentation the ovules are on a central column; example: Dianthus.

blocks.caption: Table: Common types of placentation

items.text: A pea pod shows marginal placentation: the seeds are arranged along one edge where the placenta was.
items.note: The pod makes the ventral ridge easy to visualise.

items.text: A cut tomato shows several chambers with seeds attached in the centre, a pattern of axile placentation.
items.note: Tomato is a standard example of axile placentation in ICSE work.

keyPoints: A bisexual flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx is made of sepals, corolla of petals, androecium of stamens and gynoecium of carpels.
A stamen consists of a filament and an anther; the anther has four pollen sacs in the typical case.
A carpel consists of stigma, style and ovary; the ovary contains ovules.
A bisexual flower has both androecium and gynoecium; a unisexual flower has only one.
Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on a common axis; racemose types grow on and bear flowers laterally, cymose types end in a flower.
Racemose flowers are in acropetal order; cymose flowers are in basipetal order.
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary: marginal, axile, parietal, basal and free-central.
Pea is marginal; china rose and tomato are axile; mustard and cucumber are parietal; sunflower and marigold are basal; Dianthus is free-central.
examFocus: Be able to label a flower diagram: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium, thalamus, stamen and carpel.
Give the parts of a stamen and a carpel and their roles.
Distinguish bisexual and unisexual flowers with examples.
Define inflorescence and distinguish racemose from cymose types using the fate of the main axis and the order of flowers.
For placentation, name the type, the ovary structure and one example; pea, china rose and tomato are frequent ICSE examples.

assessment.title: The Flower: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the parts, inflorescence types or placentation types clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.prompt: Name the four whorls of a bisexual flower from outside to inside.
exercises.explanation: These are the four whorls in their usual outside-to-inside order.

exercises.prompt: What is a bisexual flower? Give one example.
exercises.answer: A bisexual flower is one that has both androecium and gynoecium. An example is Hibiscus.
exercises.explanation: The definition and one suitable example carry the marks.

exercises.prompt: Name the parts of a carpel and state the function of one of them.
exercises.answer: The parts of a carpel are stigma, style and ovary. The ovary contains the ovules that become seeds after fertilisation.
exercises.explanation: All three parts should be named, and one function should be stated clearly.

exercises.prompt: What is placentation? Name two types and one example of each.
exercises.answer: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary. Marginal placentation, for example pea, and axile placentation, for example china rose, are two types.
exercises.explanation: The definition and two named types with examples are required.

exercises.answer: In racemose inflorescence the main axis continues to grow and bears flowers laterally in acropetal order, as in mustard. In cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, growth is limited, and the flowers are borne in basipetal order.
exercises.explanation: The distinction should include the fate of the main axis and the order of flowers.

exercises.prompt: How is a typical anther arranged?
exercises.answer: A typical anther is bilobed, with two lobes, and each lobe has two pollen sacs, so the anther has four pollen sacs in which pollen grains are formed.
exercises.explanation: The bilobed, two-pollen-sac-per-lobe arrangement is the standard outline.

questions.prompt: The female whorl of a bisexual flower is the:
questions.explanation: The gynoecium is the female whorl, made of one or more carpels.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing androecium — that is the male whorl.

questions.prompt: The part of a flower that produces pollen is the:
questions.explanation: The anther, which is part of the stamen, produces pollen grains.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing stigma — that receives pollen, not produces it.

questions.prompt: The swollen tip of the flower stalk on which the floral parts are arranged is the:
questions.explanation: The thalamus, or receptacle, is the platform on which the floral whorls are seated.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing placenta — that is the tissue to which ovules are attached inside the ovary.

questions.prompt: A flower that has both androecium and gynoecium is called:
questions.explanation: A bisexual flower contains both male and female whorls.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing unisexual — that has only one sex, not both.

questions.prompt: In a racemose inflorescence, the main axis:
options: Continues to grow and bears flowers laterally
questions.answer: Continues to grow and bears flowers laterally
questions.explanation: In racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal order.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing that it ends in a flower — that is the cymose pattern.

questions.prompt: Pea shows which type of placentation?
questions.explanation: Pea has a one-chambered ovary with ovules on a ventral ridge, which is marginal placentation.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing axile — that occurs in multilocular ovaries such as china rose.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the male whorl of a flower, made of stamens, is called the ________.
questions.explanation: The androecium is the male whorl, made of stamens.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'stamen' — that is the unit, while androecium is the whorl.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks: in ________ placentation the ovary is one-chambered and the ovules are borne on a ridge along the ventral suture.
questions.explanation: Marginal placentation is the one-chambered, ventral-ridge type, as in pea.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'parietal' — that has ovules on the inner wall, not on a ventral ridge.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a carpel.
questions.answer: A carpel is the female reproductive part of a flower and consists of three parts. The stigma is the top part that receives pollen. The style is the neck connecting the stigma to the ovary. The ovary is the swollen basal part that contains one or more ovules. After pollination, the pollen tube grows through the style to reach the ovary. So the carpel has stigma, style and ovary, and its role is to receive pollen and develop ovules into seeds.
questions.explanation: A good answer names all three parts and explains their arrangement and role.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting the style or confusing the stigma with the ovary.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between racemose and cymose inflorescence.
questions.answer: In racemose inflorescence the main axis continues to grow and the flowers are borne laterally in acropetal order, with the older flowers below and the younger ones above; examples include mustard and radish. In cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited, and the flowers are borne in basipetal order, with the older flowers above and the younger ones below.
questions.explanation: Both the fate of the main axis and the order of flowers should be mentioned.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that racemose is 'long' and cymose is 'short' without the growth rule and order.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a typical bisexual flower.
questions.answer: A typical bisexual flower is built on a swollen stalk tip called the thalamus, on which the parts are arranged in four concentric whorls. The outermost whorl is the calyx, made of sepals, usually green and protective in the bud. Inside it is the corolla, made of petals, often coloured and attractive to pollinators. The third whorl is the androecium, the male whorl made of stamens; each stamen has a filament and an anther, and the anther produces pollen grains, usually in four pollen sacs. The innermost whorl is the gynoecium, the female whorl made of one or more carpels; each carpel has a stigma, a style and an ovary containing ovules. Because it has both androecium and gynoecium, the flower is bisexual. The ovary, after pollination and fertilisation, develops into fruit and the ovules into seeds.
questions.explanation: A complete answer covers the thalamus, the four whorls with their parts, and the male and female roles leading to fruit and seed.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only the petals and sepals and forgetting the stamens and carpels.

questions.prompt: A flower is described as unisexual. What does this tell you about its whorls, and how is it different from a bisexual flower?
questions.answer: A unisexual flower has only one of the two reproductive whorls: it is either staminate, with only androecium, or pistillate, with only gynoecium. This means it cannot on its own carry out both the male and female parts of reproduction. A bisexual flower, by contrast, has both androecium and gynoecium in the same flower, so it has both male and female parts together. The difference is therefore in the presence or absence of one sex, not in the calyx or corolla, which may be the same in both types.
questions.explanation: The answer should focus on the whorl composition and separate that from the non-reproductive whorls.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a unisexual flower has no petals or sepals — the difference is in androecium and gynoecium, not necessarily in the perianth.
